metaTitle: Best Floor Jacks for Home Garages (2026)
metaDescription: Five hydraulic floor jacks from 2 to 4 ton compared by minimum height, lift range, weight, pump design and saddle, with advice on matching one to your car.
expertTake: The BIG RED 4 ton low profile service jack is the best all-round floor jack here: a 3-7/8 inch minimum height, a 20 inch maximum and a dual-piston pump that fits most cars, trucks and SUVs. The DNA MOTORING 2 ton is the value pick for a compact car. Skip any jack you plan to use as support, because a floor jack lifts and a pair of rated jack stands holds.
introParagraphs: A floor jack is a hydraulic lifting tool on wheels. It rolls under the car, raises one corner or one end with a few pumps of the handle and rolls out again. It is faster and safer than the scissor jack that comes with the vehicle, but it is a lifting device, not a support.

Buying one is a matching exercise. The jack must fit under the car, reach the lift point and carry the load with margin, and you have to be able to move it around the garage. This guide compares five jacks across the size classes and says which one suits which vehicle.

products.name: BIG RED 4 Ton Low Profile Dual-Piston Hydraulic Service Floor Jack
products.description:
The BIG RED 4 ton jack covers the widest range of vehicles in this guide. It lifts from 3-7/8 inches to 20 inches, which clears a lowered sedan and still reaches the frame of a full-size pickup, and the 8,000 lb rating leaves a wide margin over the weight of one corner of any passenger vehicle. A dual-piston pump raises the saddle to the load about five times faster than a single piston design, so you spend less time pumping empty air.

Steel construction and a wide stance make it heavy, and it sits in the premium price tier. Compared with the 3 ton AV Steel it lifts higher and fits lower cars, but it is a larger tool to store. If you only jack a compact car, the DNA MOTORING 2 ton is lighter and cheaper.

In ownership the main jobs are keeping the hydraulic oil topped up, wiping the ram and storing it fully lowered. Casters and a wide stance make it stable, and parts for a well-known brand are easy to source. It is the one to buy once and keep for decades.
products.bestFor: Households with a mix of cars, SUVs and trucks that need one jack.
pros: 3-7/8 in to 20 in range covers cars and trucks
Dual piston pump saves pumping effort
Wide stance steadies the lift
Brand parts and oil are easy to source

products.name: AUTOWN 3 Ton Alloy Steel Floor Jack, 7.1 to 20.9 in Lift Range
products.description:
The AUTOWN is built for taller vehicles. A 7.1 inch minimum height and 20.9 inch maximum height suit pickups, full-size SUVs and crossovers, where the lift point sits high and a low-profile jack would run out of travel. It is rated for 6,600 lb and uses an alloy steel frame, and a cross-shaped rubber pad is meant to cradle frame rails and pinch welds. A quick-lift system reduces the number of strokes before the saddle meets the load.

The 7.1 inch minimum height is the catch. It will not slide under a sports car or a lowered sedan, and compared with the BIG RED 4 ton it has no low-profile range at all. If the car is stock height or taller, that is fine, and the higher reach is worth it.

Expect to check the rubber pad for wear, and to keep the hydraulic fluid topped up. The jack is simple, and the alloy steel body is easy to keep clean. Store it lowered and upright.
products.bestFor: Pickup, SUV and crossover owners with high lift points.
pros: 20.9 in maximum height reaches high frames
Rated for 6,600 lb with a margin for SUVs
Cross-shape pad grips frame rails
Quick-lift reduces pumping strokes
cons: 7.1 in minimum will not fit low cars

products.name: DNA MOTORING 2 Ton Low Profile Hydraulic Floor Jack, 4,000 lb
products.description:
The DNA MOTORING 2 ton jack is the lightest and cheapest of the five, and it is sized for compact cars. A 5.1 inch minimum fits under most sedans and hatchbacks, a 13 inch maximum is enough for a tire change or brake job, and a built-in safety release valve triggers if you overload it. The 4,000 lb rating is more than the weight of one end of a small car.

Capacity is the limit. A 13 inch lift is too short for a truck, and 2 tons leaves little margin for a heavy SUV. Against the BIG RED 4 ton it lifts less and reaches less, but it is far easier to carry and store. If your cars are small and you want a basic jack, this is the sensible choice.

Keep the pump clean, store it lowered and top up the oil when the lift feels soft. It is not for daily shop use, but it is fine for seasonal tire swaps and driveway maintenance.
products.bestFor: Compact car owners who change tires and do brakes at home.
pros: Lightweight and easy to store
5.1 in minimum fits most sedans
Overload valve adds a safety layer
Lowest price tier in the guide
cons: 13 in maximum is too low for trucks
2 ton margin is thin for heavy SUVs
Single brand with limited long-term support

products.name: SATA 3-Ton Aluminum Floor Jack, Low Profile, Dual-Piston Rapid Lift
products.description:
The SATA aluminum jack is for people who move their jack a lot. It is made from high-strength aluminum that SATA lists as about 30 percent lighter than comparable steel, with a dual-piston rapid lift pump to cut handle effort and a 3 ton rating. Each unit is rated to 4.5 tons, 1.5 times its rated capacity, which tells you the safety margin that was designed in.

Aluminum costs more and dents more easily than steel, so it sits in the premium price tier. It is also less forgiving of rough handling at a track or in a shop. Compared with the BIG RED 4 ton steel jack it is easier to carry to a trunk, but it lifts less.

Store it on a shelf away from salt and moisture, and wipe the ram after use. Aluminum resists rust, which helps in a damp garage. If you take the jack to the track or a friend's house, the weight saving is real.
products.bestFor: People who carry the jack in a trunk or to track days.
pros: Aluminum body is far lighter than steel
Rated to 1.5 times capacity for margin
Dual piston pump cuts handle effort
Resists rust in a damp garage
cons: 3 ton rating lifts less than a 4 ton unit

products.name: AV Steel 3 Ton Single-Piston Floor Jack, 6,000 lb, 5.5 to 18.5 in
products.description:
The AV Steel 3 ton jack is the straightforward steel option for standard cars, SUVs, minivans and pickups. It lifts 6,000 lb with a range of 5.5 inches to 18.5 inches, and the maker notes it is not suited to lowered or sports cars. At 63.8 lb it is heavy, as steel jacks are, and the single-piston pump needs more strokes to reach the load than the dual-piston designs.

The trade is price and speed. It costs less than the BIG RED and the SATA, but every lift takes longer because the saddle rises slowly until it touches the frame. Compared with the AUTOWN it starts lower at 5.5 inches, so it fits more cars, but it lifts a little less at the top.

Ownership is plain: wipe the ram, store it lowered and check the oil. It is a good garage jack for a household with a standard car and an SUV, and the steel body shrugs off rough handling.
products.bestFor: Standard cars, minivans and SUVs on a steel jack budget.
pros: Steel body shrugs off rough handling
5.5 in to 18.5 in range fits most cars
6,000 lb rating covers SUVs and minivans
Lower price tier than dual-piston jacks
cons: Single piston pump is slower to rise
Will not fit lowered or sports cars

buyingCriteria.explanation: A jack lifts one end or one corner of the vehicle, not the whole weight, so a 2 ton jack is enough for most compact cars. Still, a margin matters because the load shifts as the car rises. The DNA MOTORING 2 ton fits small cars, a 3 ton unit like the AV Steel handles SUVs and minivans, and the BIG RED 4 ton covers heavier trucks. Buy a rating at least 50 percent above the lifted weight.

The minimum height is the saddle height when fully lowered, and it decides whether the jack fits under the car. The BIG RED lists 3-7/8 inches, the DNA MOTORING 5.1 inches, the AV Steel 5.5 inches and the AUTOWN 7.1 inches. Lowered cars need 3 to 4 inches, and stock sedans 5 inches. Measure the gap between the lift point and the ground before you buy.

The maximum height must clear the lift point plus the height of the jack stand. The AUTOWN lists 20.9 inches, the BIG RED 20 inches, the AV Steel 18.5 inches and the DNA MOTORING only 13 inches. A 13 inch lift is enough for a sedan but not for a pickup. Add the stand height to the lift point before you decide.

A dual-piston pump, like the BIG RED and SATA, raises the saddle quickly with a few light strokes until it meets the load, then switches to a slower high-force stage. A single-piston jack like the AV Steel needs more strokes. Over a season of tire changes the difference is a few minutes each time. Dual piston costs more but is worth it if you lift often.

Steel jacks weigh 60 to 80 pounds, like the 63.8 lb AV Steel, and tolerate abuse. Aluminum jacks like the SATA are about 30 percent lighter and resist rust, but dent more easily and cost more. If you carry the jack, aluminum is a clear win. If it stays in the garage, steel gives more value.

An overload valve, as on the DNA MOTORING, stops the jack lifting beyond its rating, and a bypass stops the ram at full extension. Neither makes the jack a support device. Always put the vehicle on rated jack stands before working under it, and never rely on hydraulics alone. A jack that creeps down under load is a sign to stop using it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit under the car
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared minimum heights from 3-7/8 inches on the BIG RED to 7.1 inches on the AUTOWN. A jack that cannot reach the lift point is useless, so range scored heavily.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lift range and capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at maximum height and rated load. The AUTOWN and BIG RED reach about 20 inches, and the DNA MOTORING reaches 13. Capacity was matched to likely vehicles.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pump and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared dual and single-piston pumps and weight. The SATA and BIG RED use dual pistons, and the AV Steel uses one and weighs 63.8 lb. Mobility and effort decided close calls.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at overload valves, saddle pads and published overload ratings. The SATA lists a 1.5x overload rating, and the DNA MOTORING has a relief valve. Always paired with jack stands.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and parts
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched price tier to build quality and parts support. The DNA MOTORING is the least expensive, and the SATA is a premium. A known brand like BIG RED earned credit for parts.

cards.label: Steel
cards.text: The BIG RED, AUTOWN, AV Steel and DNA MOTORING are steel. They are heavy but forgiving, and they cost less per ton of capacity.

cards.label: Aluminum
cards.text: The SATA is aluminum, about 30 percent lighter and rust-resistant. It costs more and dents more easily, but it is far easier to carry.

howToChoose.note: Choose steel for a garage jack, and aluminum if you move the jack often.

rows: Single piston at a lower tier

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A jack that fits under your car, reaches the lift point and is light enough to move. A rated pair of jack stands and a torque wrench matter more than extra tonnage.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DNA MOTORING 2 ton is the best fit for a compact car, and the AV Steel 3 ton for an SUV. The BIG RED covers both if you want one jack for the household.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You lift often, own taller vehicles or want a lighter jack. The BIG RED and SATA justify the cost with a dual-piston pump and a better range or weight.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You jack a car twice a year. The DNA MOTORING or AV Steel does the job without extras.

maintenance.why: Low oil makes the lift soft and the ram creep. Use jack oil, not brake fluid or motor oil, with the ram retracted.
Grit on the ram scores the seals. Wipe it clean and store it lowered.
Air in the system causes soft lifts. Open the release valve and pump the handle several times.
Dry casters bind and make the jack hard to position. A drop of light oil is enough.
A cracked weld or worn saddle is a reason to stop using the jack.

faq.q: What tonnage floor jack do I need?
faq.a: A 2 ton jack is enough for most compact cars, 3 ton for SUVs and minivans and 4 ton for heavy trucks. The jack lifts one end or corner, but leave a margin above the lifted weight.

faq.q: Is a low profile jack better?
faq.a: It is necessary for lowered cars and sports cars. For stock SUVs and trucks, minimum height is less important than maximum lift. The BIG RED lists both a low minimum and a high maximum.

faq.q: Can I work under a car on a floor jack?
faq.a: No. A floor jack lifts, and rated jack stands hold the load. Place stands under the frame or lift points before getting under the vehicle, and never rely on hydraulics alone.
Aluminum is lighter and rust-resistant, and steel is tougher and cheaper. The SATA aluminum jack is 30 percent lighter, which matters if you carry it. A garage jack can be steel.

faq.q: How do I fix a jack that will not hold pressure?
faq.a: Check the oil, bleed the air and inspect the seals. A jack that creeps down under load needs a service or replacement. Do not use it to support a vehicle.

faq.q: How long does a floor jack last?
faq.a: A well-kept steel jack can last decades. Keep the oil topped up, store it lowered and wipe the ram. Cheap jacks vary, so look for a published overload rating and a known brand.
